summary: Which receptors each beta-blocker actually hits, why each blockade produces its effect, and the three places a one-grid chart oversimplifies (selectivity is dose-dependent; the Na⁺ and K⁺ columns are the overdose / arrhythmia stories).

body.text: Why each blockade does what it does

rows: Dominant cardiac subtype — blocking it lowers cAMP-driven calcium influx in the SA node, AV node, and myocardium: slower rate, weaker contraction, slower conduction.

Mediates bronchial and skeletal-muscle vascular smooth-muscle relaxation — blockade removes that relaxation, hence bronchospasm risk in reactive airway disease and blunting of the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia.
Blockade removes peripheral arterial/venous vasoconstriction, dropping afterload directly — the extra BP-lowering effect of carvedilol and labetalol beyond β1 blockade alone.

High-dose fast-sodium-channel blockade slows phase-0 depolarization and widens the QRS. Clinically it matters most in overdose — propranolol's combined β1 + Na⁺ blockade makes it disproportionately dangerous vs cardioselective agents.

Sotalol's potassium-channel blockade is its defining class III antiarrhythmic property — it prolongs QT (therapeutic for reentrant arrhythmias, but the mechanism behind its dose-dependent torsades risk). This is why sotalol is dosed and monitored differently from other beta-blockers.
Nebivolol stimulates endothelial nitric oxide release, producing vasodilation independent of beta blockade — the basis of its comparatively neutral hemodynamic and metabolic profile.

items: 'Cardioselective' is dose-dependent, not absolute. Metoprolol, atenolol, and bisoprolol are β1-selective at typical doses, but selectivity narrows and disappears at higher doses — a 'cardioselective' agent can still provoke bronchospasm in a severe asthmatic at high enough dosing.
Nebivolol's NO-release advantage is most prominent where β1 selectivity holds; at higher doses selectivity is lost and the NO benefit is correspondingly less distinct.

Carvedilol and labetalol's α1 effect is genuinely mild (correctly not a full checkmark) but clinically real — the reason both are reasonable when you want beta blockade plus some afterload reduction without a dedicated alpha blocker's orthostatic risk.

body.text: For the toxicology of beta-blocker overdose (MSA-driven QRS widening, propranolol lipophilicity/CNS toxicity, high-dose insulin euglycemic therapy, glucagon, lipid emulsion), see the dedicated overdose reference.
